cards.title: MVT Architecture & Request-Response Lifecycle
cards.question: Explain MVT Architecture & Request-Response Lifecycle
cards.answer_30s: Django follows Model-View-Template (MVT): an HTTP request enters WSGI/ASGI -> Request Middleware -> URL Resolver -> View (controller logic) -> ORM Models / Templates -> Response Middleware -> Client.
pitfalls: Keep business logic in services/models rather than bloated views ('fat models/services, thin views').

cards.title: ORM Lazy Evaluation, `select_related` & `prefetch_related`
cards.question: Explain ORM Lazy Evaluation, `select_related` & `prefetch_related`
cards.answer_30s: Django QuerySets are lazy—they hit the DB only when evaluated (iteration, `list()`, `len()`). Prevent N+1 queries using `select_related()` (SQL JOIN for ForeignKey/OneToOne) and `prefetch_related()` (separate IN query + Python join for ManyToMany/reverse FK).
cards.typical_use: Eliminating N+1 bottlenecks in Django REST Framework endpoints.
pitfalls: Use `only()`/`defer()` or `values()`/`values_list()` when fetching a few columns from wide tables.

cards.title: Migrations & Zero-Downtime Schema Changes
cards.question: Explain Migrations & Zero-Downtime Schema Changes
cards.answer_30s: `makemigrations` diffs model definitions into versioned migration files; `migrate` applies them transactionally (on PostgreSQL). Always separate schema additions from destructive column drops across releases so rolling pods don't crash.
cards.typical_use: Safe CI/CD database deployments in Django.
pitfalls: Add `makemigrations --check` to CI so unmigrated model edits fail PRs immediately.

cards.title: `F()` Expressions, `select_for_update()` & `transaction.atomic()`
cards.question: Explain `F()` Expressions, `select_for_update()` & `transaction.atomic()`
cards.answer_30s: Reading a model field in Python, incrementing it, and calling `.save()` causes lost updates under concurrency. Use `F()` expressions for atomic SQL-level updates, or `transaction.atomic()` + `select_for_update()` for multi-step invariants.
cards.typical_use: Preventing race conditions in counters, wallets, and inventory.
pitfalls: Also use `bulk_create()` and `bulk_update()` for batch writes instead of looping `.save()`.

cards.title: CSRF, XSS, SQLi & DRF Permissions
cards.question: Explain CSRF, XSS, SQLi & DRF Permissions
cards.answer_30s: Django protects against SQLi via parameterized ORM queries, XSS via auto-escaped templates, and CSRF via `CsrfViewMiddleware` tokens on unsafe methods. In DRF, combine `IsAuthenticated` with custom object-level `has_object_permission` checks.
cards.typical_use: Securing multi-user APIs against IDOR and CSRF.
pitfalls: Never use `mark_safe()` on untrusted strings or raw SQL string formatting with `extra()` / `RawSQL()`.

cards.title: Celery Async Tasks & `transaction.on_commit()`
cards.question: Explain Celery Async Tasks & `transaction.on_commit()`
cards.answer_30s: Offload slow emails, PDFs, and webhooks to Celery workers. Always enqueue tasks inside `transaction.on_commit(lambda: task.delay(id))` so the worker never wakes up before the DB transaction commits!

code.body:
from django.db import transaction
with transaction.atomic():
    order = Order.objects.create(...)
    transaction.on_commit(lambda: send_receipt.delay(order.id))

cards.typical_use: Fixing intermittent 'ObjectDoesNotExist' race conditions in Celery workers.
pitfalls: `transaction.on_commit` is a classic senior Django production insight.

cards.title: Q: `select_related` vs `prefetch_related` — how do they work under the hood?
cards.question: Q: `select_related` vs `prefetch_related` — how do they work under the hood?
cards.answer_30s: A: `select_related` performs a single SQL INNER/LEFT JOIN (best for single-valued ForeignKey/OneToOne). `prefetch_related` runs a second query (`WHERE id IN (...)`) and joins in Python (needed for ManyToMany and reverse ForeignKey to avoid massive row multiplication).

cards.typical_use: Most asked Django ORM performance question.
pitfalls: Calling `.filter()` on a prefetched relation later still triggers a new query unless you use `Prefetch(to_attr=...)`.

cards.title: Q: What is the difference between `null=True` and `blank=True`?
cards.question: Q: What is the difference between `null=True` and `blank=True`?
cards.answer_30s: A: `null=True` is database-level (allows SQL NULL). `blank=True` is validation/form-level (allows empty input in forms/DRF serializers). For string fields (`CharField`/`TextField`), Django convention uses `blank=True, default=''` without `null=True` to avoid two representations of 'empty'.
pitfalls: Exception: if a `CharField` has `unique=True` and is optional, you DO need `null=True, blank=True` so multiple empty strings don't collide on UNIQUE.

cards.title: Q: Signals vs Overriding `save()` vs Service Layer — which do you prefer?
cards.question: Q: Signals vs Overriding `save()` vs Service Layer — which do you prefer?
cards.answer_30s: A: Signals (`post_save`) create hidden implicit side effects, make tracing/testing harder, and don't fire on bulk operations (`QuerySet.update()`/`bulk_create()`). Prefer explicit service-layer functions (or `transaction.on_commit`) for business workflows.

pitfalls: Knowing that `bulk_create` and `.update()` bypass `save()` and signals is a great practical catch.

cards.title: Q: `len(qs)` vs `qs.count()` vs `qs.exists()`?
cards.question: Q: `len(qs)` vs `qs.count()` vs `qs.exists()`?
cards.answer_30s: A: `len(qs)` fetches and instantiates EVERY matching model object into Python memory. `qs.count()` runs `SELECT COUNT(*)`. `qs.exists()` runs `SELECT 1 ... LIMIT 1` (fastest for existence checks). Exception: if you already need to iterate the queryset anyway, `len(qs)` reuses the cached result.
cards.typical_use: Avoiding accidental full-table loads in views.
pitfalls: Similarly, `if queryset:` evaluates the whole queryset—use `if queryset.exists():` if you don't need the rows.

cards.title: Q: How does Django REST Framework handle throttling, pagination, and serialization?
cards.question: Q: How does Django REST Framework handle throttling, pagination, and serialization?
cards.answer_30s: A: DRF provides `Serializer`/`ModelSerializer` for validation and JSON rendering, `PageNumber`/`CursorPagination` for bounded responses, and `AnonRateThrottle`/`UserRateThrottle` backed by Redis cache for rate limiting.

cards.title: Q: How do you test Django views and DB queries effectively?
cards.question: Q: How do you test Django views and DB queries effectively?
cards.answer_30s: A: Use `pytest-django` or `TestCase` (wraps each test in a rolled-back transaction), `assertNumQueries(N)` to catch N+1 regressions automatically in CI, and `override_settings` for isolated config tests.
pitfalls: `assertNumQueries` is one of Django's best built-in testing tools.

cards.title: Q: WSGI (Gunicorn) vs ASGI (Uvicorn/Daphne) in Django?
cards.question: Q: WSGI (Gunicorn) vs ASGI (Uvicorn/Daphne) in Django?
cards.answer_30s: A: WSGI is synchronous (one thread/worker per request). ASGI supports async views, WebSockets (Django Channels), and concurrent non-blocking I/O—though mixing sync ORM calls in async views requires `sync_to_async` or Django 4.1+/5.x async ORM methods (`aget`, `acreate`).
pitfalls: Remember Django's `async` ORM still uses sync drivers underneath unless configured carefully.
